claims.text: The two-phase coexistence simulation method can predict melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
The two-phase coexistence method reduces computational cost relative to full thermodynamic integration.
The initial state is a crystalline solid near its melting point.
The method uses an ab initio molecular-dynamics cell containing coexisting solid and liquid regions.
The coexistence simulation is performed under periodic boundary conditions.
The simulation uses fixed system size and total energy, or pressure conditions tuned to the melting point.
An interface exists between the coexisting solid and liquid regions.
Equilibration of the coexisting phases exposes the thermodynamic differences between the solid and liquid at the melting point, including latent heat and volume differences.
These coexisting-phase properties permit extraction of the melting temperature and associated fusion properties without costly free-energy integration.
The method will produce mutually consistent estimates of melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
Traditional ab initio free-energy calculations based on full thermodynamic integration require expensive molecular-dynamics sampling.
The method is best suited to materials for which stable, well-defined solid-liquid coexistence can be established.
Complex or anisotropic interface behavior may reduce the accuracy of the method.
Intricate interface structures or deviations from ideal coexistence conditions may reduce the robustness of predicted melting properties.
